title: Mina's Tiny Splash
markdown:
Books about ponds mention lilies and dragonflies. They mention less often what a bit of water and a lot of sunshine can do to a morning. This is about that, and about a mouse.

Mina liked things just so. Home under the old oak: very neat. Whiskers dusted with pollen. Heart as soft as a dandelion puff. She loved dew-kissed clover and the rustle of leaves. The village pond was another matter. Vast. Shimmering. Wet. Loud. Splashy. Thinking about it made her paws tremble. A giant watery watcher.

Her best friend Rowan the rook, shiny black feathers and a larger curiosity, flew the pond daily with news. “The frogs are practising opera. Bartholomew the Bullfrog hit a note that shattered a dewdrop.” Mina shook her head. Bartholomew’s boom near that expanse of wet made her fur prickle.

Gran Elin the badger, older than the oldest tree, sat by her burrow knitting moonlight, fur the colour of mist. She watched Mina fret. “The water is just water. Sometimes it waits. It does not hurry. Neither should you.”

One breezy spring morning a notice appeared on a sturdy reed, posted by Mr. Finnigan, swimming instructor, cheerful and orderly:

NOTICE TO ALL POND-DWELLERS
Responsible Splashing is Key to a Joyful Dip
Measured, mindful, a contribution to the atmosphere. Excessive, uncontained, disruptive: avoid.

He imagined polite ripples, delicate fountains that tickled dragonflies. The village children read it and lit up. Leo, muddy knees, declared they could splash if they did it responsibly. Lily, toes already wiggling in worn boots, said they would invent new kinds.

They did. The next afternoon the pond was a symphony with wet feet for an orchestra. Children leaped with magnificent rushes that would have failed any exam in restraint and passed every exam in joy. They invented the Rainbow Ripple, spinning in unison, water in arcs that caught the sun like a hundred small arguments for staying outside. Then the Silent Surfer, a glide with hardly a splash, to prove control, which made Mr. Finnigan almost smile before he remembered his whistle. He stood on a reedy bank looking bewildered. His notice, meant to rein things in, had become a sport with categories. He chuckled, which was not in the original plan, and wrote imaginative on a scrap as if the word might behave.

Mina watched from under a broad fern, heart thumping with each plop. Rowan landed. “A grand time. Maybe a little ripple. Tiny.”

She shook her head. Too much. Too brave, the others. The noise like thunder.

Then a Giggly Geyser — invented by a child named Llinos — sent a wave toward the bank. It did not hit Mina. A fine cool mist landed on her nose and whiskers. She blinked. Cool. Refreshing. Not a monster. Sunshine, damp earth, reeds, happy children.

The mist did not push her in. It showed her a frog splashing nearby, delighted, unmonstrous. The sound that had seemed fearsome was less powerful than the feel of the cool. Even a big noisy splash could make a gentle weather.

Mr. Finnigan, wiping spray from his spectacles, noticed her stance. “Thinking of joining? Most Imaginative Responsible Splash contest. The smallest splash can still be a good idea.”

Mina looked at her paws. “Too deep. Too splashy.”

Rowan nudged with a wing. “A mouse-sized splash. A responsible plink. A responsible drip.”

Gran Elin ambled closer and patted her head, paw soft as moss. “Biggest outings start with small steps. The pond has room for more than one kind of brave.”

Mina looked at the light on the water, at Rowan’s grin, at Gran Elin’s steady gaze. She took a deep mouse breath of damp air and scurried to the edge where the pond lapped moss. Breeze in the reeds. Cool clear water at her paw. One trembling dip, a tiny wiggle. A single droplet plinked. A fleeting ripple, a miniature echo of the grand ones.

It was hers. Responsible. Mouse-sized, and quite enough. The pond felt friendlier. The water, which had been a watcher, was just cool. A flutter of pride, bright as a kingfisher, arrived and sat down.

She logged fern-watch / Llinos geyser mist / one plink in a clover-leaf notebook no bigger than a petal, left the notice on its reed where notices belong, and let Rowan announce the plink to the frogs as if it were a small opera with excellent manners. Bartholomew, somewhere in the reeds, hit no dewdrop. Mina, who had been so afraid, had found a way to dance with the water that fitted a mouse.
